A late or missed period can be caused by many things: stress, travel, illness, or pregnancy. If you're sexually active, you might want to take a test.
If your period is more than a week late, it's worth considering a pregnancy test or consulting a doctor if you're concerned about hormonal imbalances.
Periods can be irregular due to changes in diet, exercise, or significant stress. Have you had any big changes lately?
Missing a period occasionally can be normal, but if it happens often, it's a good idea to chat with a healthcare provider about it.
Stress is a huge factor in delayed cycles. Try to relax and keep logging your symptoms so we can see the pattern.
If you suspect pregnancy, the most reliable next step is a home test or a blood test at a clinic.
If you're experiencing unusually heavy bleeding (soaking through a pad or tampon every hour), please consult a doctor immediately.
Flow can vary, but staying hydrated and getting enough iron is important if your flow is heavy. Keep an eye on any large blood clots.
You can log your flow intensity in the daily logs to track patterns over several months. This data is great to show a doctor.
Heavy bleeding can sometimes cause fatigue due to low iron. Make sure you're eating iron-rich foods like leafy greens.
Menorrhagia is the medical term for heavy periods. If you feel dizzy or very weak while bleeding, please seek medical advice.
Are you seeing clots larger than a quarter? If so, that's definitely something to mention to your gynecologist.
Feeling tired is very common during the luteal phase and menstruation. Your body is using a lot of energy! Make sure to rest.
Try to prioritize sleep and stay hydrated. Low iron during your period can also contribute to feeling exhausted.
It's okay to slow down. Listen to your body and give yourself permission to take a nap if you need one.
Hormonal shifts can definitely impact your energy levels. Magnesium-rich foods or supplements might help, but check with a pro first.
Are you getting enough rest? The app's log feature can help you see if your fatigue follows a specific pattern in your cycle.
Lower energy is a signal to nourish yourself. Consider iron-rich snacks like nuts or spinach.
Mood changes are a normal part of hormonal shifts. Be kind to yourself today.
If you're feeling irritable or sad, it might be PMS. Tracking these feelings in the 'Log Today' section can help you predict them next month.
It's completely normal to feel more emotional during certain times of your month. Remember, this phase will pass.
Hormones can be a roller coaster! Deep breathing, meditation, or just talking to a friend can sometimes help with mood swings.
Log your mood today so you can see the patterns in the Insights section. It helps to know when to expect these feelings.
You are not alone in feeling this way. Many users report similar mood shifts just before their period starts.
For cramps, try magnesium-rich foods like dark chocolate, nuts, and leafy greens.
Staying hydrated is key! Drink plenty of water and herbal teas. Avoid too much caffeine or salt if you're feeling bloated.
If you have a heavy flow, focus on iron-rich foods like spinach, beans, and lean meats to keep your energy up.
Cravings for sweets or salt are very common during PMS. It's okay to indulge a little, but try to balance it with nutritious meals.
Warm, comforting meals like soups or stews can be especially soothing during the first few days of your period.
Ginger and turmeric are great anti-inflammatory foods that might help reduce period pain.
Cervical mucus changes throughout your cycle. Clear and stretchy discharge usually means you're approaching ovulation.
White, creamy discharge is common after ovulation. However, if it's thick like cottage cheese and itchy, it could be a yeast infection.
A slight odor is normal, but a strong, 'fishy' smell or yellow/green discharge should be checked by a doctor.
Spotting between periods can happen for many reasons. Log it in your notes so you can track how often it occurs.
Healthy discharge is usually clear or white and doesn't have a strong, unpleasant smell or cause irritation.
Brown discharge is often just 'old blood' from the end of a period, but if it's persistent, mention it to a doctor.
The app always shows your status for 'Today' on the main dashboard circle.
You can see a summary of past months in the 'Cycle history' section on the home page.
Want to see the bigger picture? Click 'See all' on the cycle history box to view your calendar over time.
I use your logged dates to build a calendar tailored to your body's specific rhythm.
Check the top of the app for today's phase and the middle for the predicted start date of your next cycle.
Every day you log makes my predictions more accurate for the following months!
Period cramps can be very uncomfortable. Try a warm heating pad, light exercise, or staying extra hydrated.
To help with cramps, many users find herbal teas (like ginger or peppermint) and rest beneficial.
Cramps are a common part of the cycle, but if they stop you from doing daily activities, it's a good idea to talk to a doctor.
A warm bath or a hot water bottle on your lower abdomen can help relax the muscles and ease the pain.
Gentle movements like yoga or a short walk can sometimes help reduce the intensity of menstrual cramps.
If you get headaches or migraines during your cycle, keep track of them to see if they are related to your hormonal phases.
